results.title: Peripheral neurons: Master regulators of skin and mucosal immune response - Basso - 2019 - European Journal of Immunology - Wiley Online Library
results.content: In this review, we discuss recent advances in the neural regulation of the immune response, both in physiological and pathological contexts by taking into account the type of organs (lungs, skin and gut), subtypes of peripheral neurons (sympathetic, nociceptive and intrinsic gut neurons) or immune cells and strains of pathogens studied. Despite their primary function in the transmission of sensations, recent works have shown that peptidergic sensory neurons can be found in close proximity with tissue-resident immune cells (e.g., dendritic cells (DCs), innate lymphoid cells (ILCs) and others) and have additional crucial functions in the detection of pathogens and modulation of associated immune responses in diverse organs 13-17. Altogether, these studies strongly suggest that luminal signals could directly influence neuron-immune cells (including macrophage) interactions to regulate GI motility and tissue protection. In another independent study conducted by the group of Henrique Veiga-Fernandes, the authors assessed the ability of neuron-derived NMU to induce ILC2s activation and regulation of type 2 immune response 14. They further showed that, following activation by NMU, lung and intestinal ILC2s exhibited Extracellular Receptor Kinase (ERK) phosphorylation and activation of the calcium-calcineurin-Nuclear Factor of Activated T-cells (NFAT)-dependent signaling pathway, which is involved in the regulation of associated cell cycle, cell division and type 2 cytokines-related genes (Fig. 4C). They reported that production of IL-5 in the lungs activated sensory neurons to secrete VIP that further activated ILC2s and effector CD4+ T cells via the VIP-VIP receptor 2 (VPAC2) axis to produce inflammatory cytokines, and amplified the pathological features associated with mouse models of type 2 airway inflammation 62 (Fig. 3C). results.content: Neuron Signaling in Metabolic Regulation. This book focuses on neuron signaling in the regulation of metabolism and body weight, and especially on methods used in these studies. In the recent years, significant progress has been made in identifying specific neurons, neural pathways, and non-neuron cells in feeding regulation, as well as in delineating autonomic nervous systems targeting peripheral metabolic tissues in the regulation of energy expenditure and metabolism. This book reviews recent progress on important neuron signaling for body weight and metabolic regulation and the state-of-the-art methods that has been applied in this field, ranging from animal models with neuron-specific manipulations, pharmacology, optogenetics, in vivo Ca2+ imaging, and viral tracing. results.title: Optogenetics and Chemogenetics | Request PDF - ResearchGate
results.content: Chemogenetics is a technique for activating or inhibiting the electrical activity of neurons and other populations of excitable cells through the interaction of specific ligands with genetically encoded receptors heterologously expressed in the target cells. Among these techniques, optogenetics and chemogenetics stand out as crucial and frequently employed methods in the investigation of neural circuits and functions because of their ability to specifically modulate the activity of neurons and neural circuits (Vlasov et al., 2018). In this context, two sophisticated methodologies, optogenetics and chemogenetics, have emerged as vital tools for recording and modulating the activity of specific neuronal populations or circuits within distinct brain regions. The utilization of AAV-mediated delivery for optogenetic and chemogenetic tools offers precise manipulation of neuronal activity, facilitating the exploration of neural circuit dynamics and behavior in both healthy and pathological conditions. results.title: neuromedin-u-programs-eosinophils-to-promote-mucosal-immunity-of-the-small-intestine - Ask this paper | Bohrium
results.content: **研究方向：**NMUR1 expression in SI eosinophils ｜ Function of NMUR1 in eosinophil responses ｜ Role of eosinophils in mucosal immunity. The tissue-derived cues regulating eosinophil responses in the SI are poorly understood. Neuromedin U receptor 1 (NMUR1), a receptor for neuromedin U (NMU), has been linked to type 2 immune responses, but its role in SI eosinophils is unknown. However, recent studies have reported that eosinophils do not express NMUR1, making the direct regulation of eosinophil responses by NMU controversial. Additionally, the cell-intrinsic roles of NMUR1 in SI eosinophils have not been explored. Various experiments, including cell transfer, stimulation with different agents, and the generation of knockout and chimeric mouse models, were conducted to investigate the ontogeny, expression dynamics, and function of NMUR1 in SI eosinophils. NMUR1 was identified as one of the most distinctively expressed genes in SI eosinophils. NMUR1-expressing SI eosinophils (NMUR1+ eosinophils) exhibited a distinct transcriptional state, with down-regulation of genes involved in proinflammatory cytokine signaling and cell adhesion, and up-regulation of genes related to cholesterol biosynthesis and degranulation. NMUR1 supported the maintenance of eosinophil numbers in the SI in a cell-intrinsic manner and promoted their degranulation. The study demonstrated that NMUR1 expression occurs in SI eosinophils, in addition to ILC2s. NMUR1-mediated signaling in eosinophils contributes to goblet cell differentiation in the steady-state SI, and future studies are needed to determine the roles of degranulation and cholesterol biosynthesis pathways in regulating goblet cell differentiation. Overall, NMUR1 signaling drives a tissue-specific program in SI eosinophils to regulate goblet cell differentiation under homeostasis. Eosinophils are granulocytes that play an essential role in type 2 immunity and regulate multiple homeostatic processes in the small intestine (SI). However, the signals that regulate eosinophil activity in the SI at steady state remain poorly understood. Through transcriptome profiling of eosinophils from various mouse tissues, we found that a subset of SI eosinophils expressed neuromedin U (NMU) receptor 1 (NMUR1). Fate-mapping analyses showed that NMUR1 expression in SI eosinophils was programmed by the local microenvironment and further enhanced by inflammation. Thus, NMU regulates epithelial cell differentiation and barrier immunity by stimulating NMUR1-expressing eosinophils in the SI, which highlights the importance of neuroimmune-epithelial cross-talk in maintaining tissue homeostasis.
